_comment: The change ledger — the single source of truth for every versioned fact on this site. Topic pages embed a record with <div class="change" data-change="<id>">; deprecations.html, timeline.html and migrations.html are generated from these same records, so the ledger can never drift from the prose. Fields: since/deprecated/removed are release lines of `tool` (major, or major.minor where the minor is the line — Spring Boot 4.1, jOOQ 3.21; null = not applicable). For tool 'spring' they are Spring BOOT lines even when the change belongs to Framework or Security — the title and why carry the library's own version. `migration` is the exact command that automates the change, if one exists. `docs` are ids into links.json. code.lang optionally overrides the sample language for the card (default per tool in changes.js).

changes.title: Getting a dependency
changes.now: inject(HttpClient) as a field initialiser
changes.was: constructor(private http: HttpClient)
changes.why: Works in functions and field initialisers, not just constructors — which is what makes functional guards, functional interceptors and reusable composables possible at all. It also drops the constructor boilerplate and plays better with inheritance.

changes.title: Declaring a component
changes.now: Standalone by default — no `standalone: true`, no NgModule
changes.was: standalone: true written explicitly (v15–18), or declared in an NgModule (pre-v15)
changes.why: NgModules existed to tell the compiler what a template could see. Standalone components carry their own `imports` array, so the indirection was pure overhead. v14 previewed it, v15 stabilised it, v19 made it the default and made the flag redundant.

changes.title: Conditionals and loops in a template
changes.now: @if / @for / @switch — built into the template language
changes.was: *ngIf / *ngFor / *ngSwitch structural directives, imported from CommonModule
changes.why: Built-in syntax needs no imports, type-narrows properly inside the block, and lets the compiler generate far less code. @for also *requires* a track expression, which turns the most common Angular performance bug into a compile error.

code.was:
{{ u.name }}

Signed out
  • {{ item.label }}

changes.title: Holding reactive state
changes.now: signal() / computed() / effect()
changes.was: A plain field plus manual change detection, or a BehaviorSubject you had to subscribe to
changes.why: Signals track their own readers, so Angular knows exactly which views depend on which state — that is the mechanism zoneless change detection is built on. They arrived in preview in v16 and stabilised in v20.

changes.title: Declaring an input
changes.now: input() / input.required() — a signal you read with ()
changes.was: @Input() decorator on a plain field
changes.why: A signal input is readable in computed() and effect() without a setter or ngOnChanges, and input.required() makes a missing input a compile-time error rather than an undefined at runtime.

changes.title: Declaring a service
changes.now: @Service()
changes.was: @Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
changes.why: Root-provided was what almost every service wanted, so v22 made it the shape of the decorator rather than an option you configure. @Service() is auto-provided by default; pass { autoProvided: false } for a service that must be listed in a providers array, or { factory } to build it from a function.

changes.title: Running code at startup
changes.now: provideAppInitializer(() => …)
changes.was: { provide: APP_INITIALIZER, useFactory: …, multi: true }
changes.why: The token form needed multi: true and a factory, and forgetting either failed silently at runtime rather than at compile time. The provide* functions take the callback directly. The same swap applies to ENVIRONMENT_INITIALIZER and PLATFORM_INITIALIZER.

changes.title: Declaring an output
changes.now: output<T>()
changes.was: @Output() name = new EventEmitter<T>()
changes.why: An output is not a stream you subscribe to, so modelling it as an EventEmitter (an RxJS Subject) always promised more than it delivered. output() exposes only emit(), which is the entire API a component actually needs, and it cannot be accidentally subscribed to or completed.

changes.title: Referencing a child element or component
changes.now: viewChild() / viewChildren() / contentChild() — signals
changes.was: @ViewChild() / @ContentChild() decorators, with a static flag and a lifecycle hook to wait for
changes.why: The decorator form set a plain property at some point during a lifecycle hook, so reading it too early gave you undefined and the fix was to know which hook. A signal query is just a signal: read it whenever, use it in computed(), and the timing question disappears along with the static flag.

changes.title: Loading part of a template lazily
changes.now: @defer with a trigger
changes.was: A route-level lazy load, or a manual dynamic import plus ViewContainerRef
changes.why: Lazy loading used to be something you could only do at a routing boundary. @defer moves it into the template, so a heavy chart or a rarely-opened dialog is split out of the bundle without restructuring the application around it. The dependencies used only inside the block go with it automatically.

changes.title: Naming a value inside a template
changes.now: @let name = expression;
changes.was: *ngIf="expr as name", or a wrapper <ng-container> whose only job was to hold the alias
changes.why: Aliasing used to be a side effect of a structural directive, which meant you needed a conditional you did not want in order to name a value you did. Worse, *ngIf's alias silently dropped the block when the value was falsy — 0 and '' vanished. @let just declares a name.

code.was: {{ user.name }}

changes.title: Unsubscribing in a component
changes.now: takeUntilDestroyed()
changes.was: takeUntil(this.destroy$) with a manual Subject and ngOnDestroy
changes.why: No boilerplate Subject, no lifecycle hook to forget. It ties to DestroyRef, so it also works in services and functions — anywhere with an injection context — not just components.

changes.title: Default change detection strategy
changes.now: OnPush — applied automatically when changeDetection is not set
changes.was: Default (check-everything) unless you opted into ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush by hand
changes.why: The old default re-checked every binding in the tree on every event. OnPush was always the right answer for signal-based components, so v22 stopped making you ask for it.

changes.title: Building a form
changes.now: form(model) — the model signal is the form
changes.was: new FormGroup({ … }) — a parallel model you kept in sync by hand
changes.why: A reactive form was a second copy of your data with its own type, its own change stream and its own ideas about validity, and half of form code existed to keep the two in step. form() takes your existing model signal as the source of truth and does not copy it — writing through the field writes the model. Validation is declared against typed paths, so a renamed property is a compile error rather than a string that silently stops matching.

changes.title: Knowing when to re-render
changes.now: Zoneless — signals tell Angular what changed
changes.was: zone.js patching every async browser API to guess that something might have changed
changes.why: zone.js monkey-patched setTimeout, addEventListener, fetch and the rest so Angular could re-check the entire component tree whenever any of them fired. It worked without you thinking about it, at the cost of ~13KB, a patched global environment that confused debuggers and third-party libraries, and change detection runs triggered by events that changed nothing. Signals carry the information directly, so the guessing is unnecessary. Experimental in v18 as provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection, stable without the prefix in v20.2, and the default for new applications from v21.

changes.title: Loading data for the current state
changes.now: httpResource() / resource() — value, isLoading and error as signals
changes.was: A subscription in ngOnInit writing to three separate fields, or an Observable plus the async pipe
changes.why: Every codebase reinvented the same trio of loading/error/value fields, and every one of them got cancellation slightly wrong — a slow response for user 1 arriving after you had already switched to user 2. A resource re-runs when its reactive request changes and abandons the previous result, so the out-of-order case cannot happen. In preview from v19; stable in v22.

changes.title: Intercepting HTTP requests
changes.now: A function, registered with withInterceptors([…])
changes.was: A class implementing HttpInterceptor, registered against the HTTP_INTERCEPTORS multi token
changes.why: The class form needed a DI registration with multi: true that was easy to get wrong and failed silently when you did. A functional interceptor is a function that calls inject() for what it needs — and because ordering is the array's order, the sequence is visible at the call site instead of depending on provider registration order.

changes.title: Guarding a route
changes.now: A function typed CanActivateFn
changes.was: A class implementing the CanActivate interface
changes.why: A guard is one decision, so a whole class with a constructor to get its dependencies was ceremony. The class-based interfaces were deprecated in v15 and removed in v16 — this is one of the few Angular changes with a hard deadline attached, so code still using them will not compile on a supported version.

changes.title: Reading a route parameter
changes.now: A component input, bound automatically by the router
changes.was: Subscribing to ActivatedRoute.paramMap
changes.why: A route parameter is data arriving from outside the component, which is exactly what an input is. With withComponentInputBinding() the router binds params, query params, data and resolved values straight to matching inputs — so the component stops depending on the router at all, which also makes it trivial to test.

changes.title: Turning on incremental hydration
changes.now: Nothing — provideClientHydration() enables it
changes.was: provideClientHydration(withIncrementalHydration())
changes.why: Incremental hydration graduated from opt-in feature to default behaviour in v22, so the feature flag that switched it on became noise. withIncrementalHydration() is deprecated and can simply be deleted.

code.now: provideClientHydration(withEventReplay())
code.was: provideClientHydration(withEventReplay(), withIncrementalHydration())

changes.title: HttpClient's transport
changes.now: fetch by default
changes.was: XMLHttpRequest by default; fetch opt-in via withFetch()
changes.why: fetch is the platform standard, works in more runtimes, and is what SSR needs. v22 flipped the default; a migration exists for anyone who still depends on XHR-specific behaviour.

changes.title: The unit test runner
changes.now: Vitest via the @angular/build:unit-test builder
changes.was: Karma + Jasmine via @angular-devkit/build-angular:karma
changes.why: Karma drives a real browser per run and predates the Vite-based build pipeline Angular now uses; Vitest reuses that pipeline, so tests start in a fraction of the time. v21 shipped the unified builder and made Vitest the default for new projects. Karma still runs — the same builder accepts runner: 'karma' — but is deprecated and takes no new features. Note that the schematic converts your Jasmine *assertions*; switching the runner itself is a one-line change to angular.json.

changes.title: Turning an Observable into a Promise
changes.now: firstValueFrom(obs) / lastValueFrom(obs)
changes.was: obs.toPromise()
changes.why: toPromise() was ambiguous about which value you wanted and resolved to undefined — silently — when the source completed empty. The replacements make the choice explicit and reject with EmptyError instead of handing you undefined.

code.now: const user = await firstValueFrom(this.http.get<User>('/me'));
code.was: const user = await this.http.get<User>('/me').toPromise();

changes.title: Retrying with a delay
changes.now: retry({ count, delay })
changes.was: retryWhen(errors => errors.pipe(delay(1000)))
changes.why: retryWhen exposed a notifier Observable that almost everybody used incorrectly — completing it silently stopped retrying, and errors in the notifier were easy to swallow. The config object covers the real use cases directly.

changes.title: Applying operators
changes.now: source.pipe(map(…), filter(…))
changes.was: source.map(…).filter(…), after importing 'rxjs/add/operator/map'
changes.why: Patching operators onto Observable.prototype meant one import anywhere in the application changed the type for everyone — and made the library impossible to tree-shake, so you shipped all of RxJS whether you used three operators or ninety. Pipeable operators are plain functions: importable, tree-shakeable, and testable on their own.

changes.title: Flattening with unbounded concurrency
changes.now: mergeMap
changes.was: flatMap
changes.why: Two names for one operator. `mergeMap` won because it names what it does — it merges the inner streams — and matches the `merge` family. `flatMap` remains as an alias and is scheduled for removal in v8.

changes.title: Mapping to a constant
changes.now: map(() => value) and switchMap(() => obs)
changes.was: mapTo(value) and switchMapTo(obs)
changes.why: The *To variants saved a few characters and doubled the API surface, and people reached for them without noticing that the argument is evaluated eagerly — switchMapTo(this.load()) calls load() once, at pipe-construction time, not per emission. Removing them removes that trap.

code.now:
clicks.pipe(map(() => 'clicked'));
clicks.pipe(switchMap(() => this.load()));
code.was:
clicks.pipe(mapTo('clicked'));
clicks.pipe(switchMapTo(this.load())); // load() ran once, up front

changes.title: Reading a stream in a template
changes.now: toSignal(obs$) — read it like any other signal
changes.was: The async pipe, or a manual subscribe into a field
changes.why: The async pipe works, but a value read three times in a template means three subscriptions unless you remember to share, and it cannot be read from component code at all. toSignal subscribes once, unsubscribes with the injection context, and gives you a plain signal usable everywhere — including inside computed().

changes.title: Configuring a multi-package test setup
changes.now: The projects option inside the root config
changes.was: A separate vitest.workspace.ts file
changes.why: Two files described one thing. Folding projects into the root config removed a whole category of "which file wins?" confusion. Deprecated in 3.2, gone in 4.

code.was:
// vitest.workspace.ts
export default ['packages/*']

changes.title: Running tests in a real browser
changes.now: Browser Mode (stable) with a provider package: @vitest/browser-playwright
changes.was: Experimental Browser Mode with the provider named as a string
changes.why: Browser Mode left experimental in v4, and providers moved into their own packages so you install only the driver you actually use rather than pulling every option into the dependency tree.

changes.title: Dependency install scripts
changes.now: Blocked by default; opt packages in explicitly
changes.was: Every dependency's preinstall/install/postinstall ran automatically
changes.why: A postinstall script is arbitrary code execution at install time, and the Rspack supply-chain attack used exactly that to ship a cryptominer. pnpm 10 turned it off by default. In v10 you allow-listed with pnpm.onlyBuiltDependencies; v11 removed that whole family — onlyBuiltDependencies, onlyBuiltDependenciesFile, neverBuiltDependencies, ignoredBuiltDependencies and ignoreDepScripts are all gone — and replaced them with a single allowBuilds list. v11 also defaults strictDepBuilds to true, so a package needing a build that you have not allowed is an error rather than a warning.

code.now:
# pnpm 11 — pnpm-workspace.yaml
allowBuilds:
  - esbuild
  - fsevents

changes.title: Where pnpm settings live
changes.now: pnpm-workspace.yaml (per project) and ~/.config/pnpm/config.yaml (global)
changes.was: The pnpm field in package.json, and .npmrc
changes.why: pnpm's settings had been squatting in two files owned by other tools. v11 split them cleanly: .npmrc keeps registry and auth settings, everything pnpm-specific moves to YAML. Environment variables moved too — npm_config_* is no longer read, use pnpm_config_*.

code.now:
# pnpm-workspace.yaml
packages:
  - 'packages/*'
allowBuilds:
  - esbuild

changes.title: A reproducible install in CI
changes.now: pnpm ci
changes.was: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
changes.why: The flag form worked but had to be remembered, and forgetting it in CI means the lockfile can be silently rewritten by the build — which is exactly the thing a lockfile exists to prevent. v11 added a first-class command, matching what npm and yarn already had. The flag still works.

code.now: pnpm ci
code.was: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

changes.title: Protection against a compromised release
changes.now: On by default — a 24-hour quarantine on new versions
changes.was: Nothing; a version published a minute ago was installable a minute ago
changes.why: Most supply-chain compromises are caught and yanked within hours, so simply not installing anything published in the last day removes most of the exposure for free. v11 defaults minimumReleaseAge to 1440 minutes and blockExoticSubdeps to true, the latter rejecting transitive dependencies that resolve to a git URL or tarball rather than the registry. Expect a CI surprise the first time you try to install a package published this morning.

code.now:
# pnpm-workspace.yaml — defaults in v11, shown explicitly
minimumReleaseAge: 1440
blockExoticSubdeps: true

# packages you need without waiting out the quarantine
minimumReleaseAgeExclude:
  - '@my-org/*'
code.was: # no equivalent — anything on the registry installed immediately

changes.title: The compiler your build runs
changes.now: K2 — the rewritten frontend, default on every 2.x toolchain
changes.was: K1, the 1.x frontend
changes.why: K2 rebuilt the compiler frontend on one semantic model (FIR): JetBrains' published benchmarks measured clean builds up to ~94% faster, and every language feature since 2.0 — guard conditions, context parameters — exists only on K2. 1.9 is the last K1 line: staying there means no fixes and a growing feature gap.

changes.title: One when branch, one extra condition
changes.now: Guard conditions: is Rainy if it.mmPerHour > 30 ->
changes.was: A nested if inside the branch, or the when flattened into booleans
changes.why: Stable in 2.2 after previewing in 2.1. The subject check and its refinement collapse into one readable branch, and exhaustiveness checking on the subject still applies — the else-less when keeps working.

changes.title: break and continue from inside a lambda
changes.now: Non-local break/continue: loop control passes through inline lambdas
changes.was: return@forEach labels and boolean flags to fake loop control
changes.why: Non-local return through an inline lambda always worked; break and continue joined it in 2.2 (previewed in 2.1). Inside a lambda passed to an inline function, they now control the nearest enclosing real loop.

changes.title: A literal $ inside a string template
changes.now: Multi-dollar interpolation: $$"…" makes a single $ literal
changes.was: ${'$'} contortions or concatenation
changes.why: With $$ before the opening quote, interpolation needs $$ and a lone $ is just a character — which is exactly what JSON-schema documents, Gradle version catalogs in scripts, and regex-heavy strings needed.

code.now:
val schema = $$"""
    { "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema",
      "maxItems": $$maxItems }
"""
code.was:
val schema = """
    { "${'$'}schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema",
      "maxItems": $maxItems }
"""

changes.title: Dependencies a call needs but should not pass by hand
changes.now: context(tx: DSLContext) fun … — provided once with with(…) at the call site
changes.was: An explicit first parameter threaded through every signature
changes.why: Preview in 2.2, stable in 2.4. Context parameters declare requirements — a transaction handle, a logger, a request scope — that the caller provides once with with(...), instead of every function in the chain carrying them. The older 'context receivers' experiment was withdrawn; this is the shipped form.

code.was:
fun insertUser(tx: DSLContext, user: NewUser): UserRecord =
    tx.insertInto(USERS).set(user.toRecord())
      .returning().fetchSingle()

db.transaction { cfg ->
    insertUser(cfg.dsl(), user)
    insertAudit(cfg.dsl(), "user created")
}

changes.title: Annotation processing on Kotlin
changes.now: KSP — KSP2, on its own 2.3.x version line
changes.was: kapt, generating Java stubs so javac processors could run
changes.why: kapt is officially in maintenance mode: it still works (the K2 implementation became the default in 2.1.20) but gets no new features. KSP processes Kotlin symbols directly instead of faking Java, which is roughly twice as fast — and since KSP 2.3.0 (Oct 2025) its version no longer needs to match your Kotlin version, so a Kotlin bump no longer waits on a KSP release.

changes.title: Nullability of the Java APIs you call
changes.now: JSpecify annotations are enforced — a violation is a compile error
changes.was: Platform types: Java values were trusted, and failed at runtime
changes.why: Kotlin 2.1 turned strict mode for JSpecify annotations on by default, and Spring Framework 7 annotated its entire API surface with them — so the framework you call most now tells the compiler exactly what can be null. Code that would have NPE'd on a platform type stops compiling instead of stopping production.

changes.title: Kotlin interfaces, seen from Java
changes.now: Interface methods with bodies compile to JVM default methods
changes.was: Synthetic DefaultImpls classes Java callers had to know about
changes.why: Java code calling a Kotlin interface finally sees an ordinary default method instead of Interface.DefaultImpls.method(instance). 2.2 made -Xjvm-default=all-compatibility the default, keeping binary compatibility with implementations compiled before the switch.

changes.title: Handling blocking requests at scale
changes.now: spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true (Java 21+): a virtual thread per request
changes.was: Tuning a platform thread pool — or rewriting the service on WebFlux for throughput
changes.why: Virtual threads make thread-per-request cheap: one property switches Tomcat/Jetty request processing, @Async and the application task executor. The scalability argument for going reactive disappears for plain blocking services — keep coroutines and Flow for structure, streaming and cancellation, not for thread economics.

code.now:
# application.yaml — Boot 3.2+, running on Java 21+
spring:
  threads:
    virtual:
      enabled: true
code.was:
# guessing at pool sizes
server:
  tomcat:
    threads:
      max: 800

changes.title: The javax → jakarta namespace break
changes.now: jakarta.* imports — Jakarta EE (Servlet 6+, Validation 3+)
changes.was: javax.servlet, javax.validation, javax.persistence…
changes.why: Java EE moved to the Eclipse Foundation and the javax trademark stayed behind, so the packages had to rename. Boot 3.0 / Framework 6.0 crossed that line (with the Java 17 baseline) and the two worlds cannot mix on one classpath — which is why every library had to publish a jakarta build, and why ancient transitive dependencies still break Boot upgrades today.

code.now:
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest
import jakarta.validation.constraints.NotBlank
code.was:
import javax.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest
import javax.validation.constraints.NotBlank

changes.title: What a starter pulls in
changes.now: Focused modules: spring-boot-starter-webmvc, per-technology spring-boot-<tech> jars
changes.was: spring-boot-starter-web and one monolithic autoconfigure jar
changes.why: Boot 4.0 split the monolith into technology modules (org.springframework.boot.<tech> packages) with matching starters and test starters. spring-boot-starter-web is deprecated in favour of -webmvc; Flyway and Liquibase now need their own starter instead of riding along. spring-boot-starter-classic restores the old everything-available classpath as a migration aid — a bridge, not a destination.

changes.title: Binding configuration to types
changes.now: @ConfigurationProperties on an immutable Kotlin data class — constructor binding by default
changes.was: A mutable JavaBean full of setters, or @Value scattered across fields
changes.why: Since Boot 3, a single-constructor type binds through its constructor with no @ConstructorBinding ceremony — so configuration becomes an immutable value object, validated once at startup, instead of mutable state any bean can poke. @Value survives for one-off reads, not for modelling config.

changes.title: Calling another service from blocking code
changes.now: RestClient — fluent, synchronous, built on the same infrastructure
changes.was: RestTemplate — in maintenance mode since Framework 5, deprecated in the 7.x docs
changes.why: RestTemplate was declared feature-complete years ago, and WebClient forced a reactive stack onto callers who only wanted a nicer API. RestClient (Framework 6.1 / Boot 3.2) is that nicer API without the reactive tax — and under virtual threads, blocking calls scale anyway. Framework 7 documents RestTemplate as deprecated, with @Deprecated planned for 7.1.

code.now:
val client = builder.baseUrl("https://api.example.com").build()

val user: User = client.get()
    .uri("/users/{id}", id)
    .retrieve()
    .body(User::class.java)!!
code.was:
val user = restTemplate.getForObject(
    "https://api.example.com/users/{id}",
    User::class.java, id)!!

changes.title: Declaring a client instead of writing one
changes.now: @HttpExchange interfaces, registered in groups with @ImportHttpServices
changes.was: A hand-written client class per remote service, wrapping RestTemplate or WebClient
changes.why: The @HttpExchange annotations existed since Framework 6.0, but Framework 7 made them first-class citizens: @ImportHttpServices registers a whole group of interfaces as beans, with per-group base URLs and client customisation — so the boilerplate client class disappears and the wire contract lives in one annotated interface.

changes.title: Versioning an HTTP API
changes.now: First-class: version on the mapping, strategy in configuration
changes.was: Hand-rolled /v2/ URL prefixes and header parsing in filters
changes.why: Framework 7 added API versioning to MVC and WebFlux — mappings declare the version they serve, spring.mvc.apiversion.* picks the resolution strategy (header, query parameter, path segment or media-type parameter), and deprecation can be signalled to clients. The clients (RestClient, WebClient, HTTP interfaces) and the test support understand versions too.

code.now:
@GetMapping("/orders/{id}", version = "2")
fun orderV2(@PathVariable id: OrderId): OrderV2 = …

# application.yaml
# spring.mvc.apiversion.use.header: API-Version
code.was:
@GetMapping("/v2/orders/{id}")   // convention, enforced nowhere
fun orderV2(@PathVariable id: OrderId): OrderV2 = …

changes.title: The Jackson you import
changes.now: tools.jackson.* — Jackson 3, an immutable mapper built via JsonMapper.builder()
changes.was: com.fasterxml.jackson.* — Jackson 2, a mutable ObjectMapper you configure after construction
changes.why: Jackson 3 (GA Oct 2025) moved Java packages and Maven groups to tools.jackson.* — except the annotations, which stay at com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation precisely so 2 and 3 can coexist on one classpath while libraries migrate. The mapper is immutable once built, JacksonException is unchecked, and java.time/Optional/parameter-names support merged into databind instead of being three add-on modules.

code.now:
import tools.jackson.databind.json.JsonMapper

val mapper = JsonMapper.builder()
    .findAndAddModules()
    .build()   // immutable from here
code.was:
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper

val mapper = ObjectMapper()
mapper.registerModule(JavaTimeModule())   // mutate-after-build
mapper.disable(WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS)

changes.title: What Jackson does when you don't configure it
changes.now: Unknown properties ignored; dates as ISO-8601 strings; enums via toString
changes.was: Unknown properties threw; dates as epoch timestamps; enums by name
changes.why: Jackson 3 flipped the defaults nearly every codebase flipped manually: FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES off (tolerant reading), WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS off (ISO strings), enum round-tripping via toString on, FAIL_ON_TRAILING_TOKENS on (stricter about garbage after the document). Audit any code that relied on the old behaviour rather than configuring it explicitly.

changes.title: Kotlin data classes and Jackson
changes.now: tools.jackson.module:jackson-module-kotlin — strict null checks on by default
changes.was: The 2.x Kotlin module — a non-null Kotlin field could still receive a JSON null
changes.why: The 3.x Kotlin module versions with the Jackson 3 line and turns StrictNullChecks and singleton support on by default — a JSON null landing in a non-null constructor parameter now fails at parse time with a clear error instead of surfacing later as an impossible NPE.

changes.title: Customising JSON in Boot
changes.now: JsonMapperBuilderCustomizer beans and @JacksonComponent
changes.was: Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer and @JsonComponent
changes.why: Boot 4 wires Jackson 3 by default, and the customisation surface renamed with it: builder customizers target JsonMapper.builder(), @JsonComponent became @JacksonComponent, and the JSON-specific properties moved under spring.jackson.json.read/write. Jackson 2 remains available during migration via the spring-boot-jackson2 module and spring.jackson.use-jackson2-defaults — but Framework 7 plans to stop auto-detecting Jackson 2 in 7.1 and drop it in 7.2, so treat those as exits, not homes.

changes.title: Plain SQL without jOOQ
changes.now: JdbcClient — fluent, named parameters, mapped to data classes
changes.was: JdbcTemplate with positional ? params and RowMapper boilerplate
changes.why: For the one-off query that doesn't warrant jOOQ's codegen, JdbcClient (Framework 6.1) gives named parameters and a fluent mapping API over the same infrastructure. JdbcTemplate is not deprecated — JdbcClient is just the version of it you'd design today.

code.now:
val count = jdbc.sql("select count(*) from orders where status = :s")
    .param("s", status)
    .query(Int::class.java)
    .single()
code.was:
val count = jdbcTemplate.queryForObject(
    "select count(*) from orders where status = ?",
    Int::class.java, status)

changes.title: Configuring HTTP security
changes.now: A SecurityFilterChain bean, written in the lambda DSL
changes.was: Subclassing WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter
changes.why: The adapter was deprecated in Security 5.7 (Boot 2.7) and removed in Security 6 (Boot 3): configuration became ordinary beans you compose instead of a template class you override. Security 7 (Boot 4) finished the story by making the lambda DSL the only DSL.

changes.title: Chaining security config with .and()
changes.now: Gone — each concern is one lambda block; authorizeHttpRequests replaces authorizeRequests
changes.was: http.authorizeRequests()…​.and().csrf()…​.and() chains
changes.why: Security 6.1 deprecated the non-lambda methods; Security 7 (Boot 4) removed them along with authorizeRequests(). The lambda DSL makes nesting explicit and closes the class of bugs where an .and() attached configuration to the wrong parent.

changes.title: Passwordless sign-in
changes.now: Built in: webAuthn { } (passkeys) and one-time-token login
changes.was: Custom filters around third-party WebAuthn libraries
changes.why: Security 6.4 (Boot 3.4) shipped passkey support in the DSL, backed by WebAuthn4J, plus magic-link style one-time tokens — the two passwordless flows teams were hand-rolling.

changes.title: Instrumenting code once
changes.now: The Micrometer Observation API — one Observation yields metrics and a span
changes.was: A Timer for the metric and manual tracer code for the span, kept in sync by hope
changes.why: Boot 3 rebuilt instrumentation on Observation: wrap the operation once, and registered handlers project it into Micrometer metrics and Micrometer Tracing spans consistently — same names, same tags, no drift between the two.

changes.title: Log output machines can read
changes.now: Built in: logging.structured.format.console=ecs (or logstash, gelf)
changes.was: A logstash-logback-encoder dependency and a logback-spring.xml per service
changes.why: Boot 3.4 made structured logging a property instead of a project: pick Elastic Common Schema, Logstash or GELF shapes for console or file, keep MDC and correlation ids, and delete the XML.

code.now:
logging:
  structured:
    format:
      console: ecs
code.was:
<!-- logback-spring.xml -->
<appender name="json"
    class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
  <encoder class="net.logstash.logback.encoder.LogstashEncoder"/>
</appender>

changes.title: Shipping telemetry over OTLP
changes.now: spring-boot-starter-opentelemetry — metrics and traces, OTEL_* env vars honoured
changes.was: A hand-assembled stack: tracing bridge, exporters and registry wired one property at a time
changes.why: Boot 4.0 collected the OpenTelemetry pieces into one starter; 4.1 made the fired-up SDK read the standard OTEL_* environment variables, so the same container config works for a Boot app as for everything else in the cluster.

changes.title: Mocking a bean in a Spring test
changes.now: @MockitoBean / @MockitoSpyBean — Framework-provided
changes.was: @MockBean / @SpyBean — Boot's own, since removed
changes.why: Framework 6.2 absorbed the idea and Boot deprecated its annotations in 3.4, then removed them in 4.0. Mind the differences while migrating: @MockitoBean does not work on @Configuration classes, and reusable setups move to the class-level types attribute.

changes.title: Pointing tests at a Testcontainers database
changes.now: @ServiceConnection on the container — Boot derives url, user, password
changes.was: @DynamicPropertySource methods copying container properties by hand
changes.why: The container itself is the source of truth for its coordinates, so Boot 3.1 taught autoconfiguration to read them directly. The property-copying ceremony — and the typos in it — disappear.

changes.title: Calling your app from a test
changes.now: RestTestClient — one fluent client, bound to MockMvc or a live server
changes.was: Two idioms: TestRestTemplate against a port, MockMvc's perform/andExpect for mock requests
changes.why: Framework 7 gave the blocking world what WebTestClient gave the reactive one: the same fluent request/assertion API whether the target is a mock servlet environment, a running server on a random port, or a plain controller instance. Boot 4 autowires it in @SpringBootTest.

changes.title: Running the build tool itself
changes.now: Gradle 9 — needs Java 17+ to run; scripts compile on Kotlin 2.2 (DSL) and Groovy 4
changes.was: Gradle 8 — ran on Java 8+, Kotlin 1.9-era DSL, Groovy 3
changes.why: The 9.0 jump (July 2025) modernised the tool's own platform: a Java 17 floor for the daemon, current Kotlin in build scripts, Groovy 4. Nothing about your application's Java version changes — the daemon JVM and your toolchain JVM are separate decisions.

code.now:
./gradlew wrapper --gradle-version 9.7.0
# then commit gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties
code.was: distributionUrl=.../gradle-8.14.5-bin.zip

changes.title: The language of build scripts
changes.now: Kotlin DSL (build.gradle.kts) — the default for new builds
changes.was: Groovy (build.gradle)
changes.why: Since 8.2, gradle init generates Kotlin DSL — typed accessors, IDE completion and refactoring across build code, and one language for app and build. Groovy scripts keep working indefinitely; the choice only really costs when a build mixes both and every snippet must be translated on the way in.

changes.title: Where dependency versions live
changes.now: gradle/libs.versions.toml — one catalog, typed libs.* accessors
changes.was: ext {} property maps, buildSrc constants objects, versions repeated per module
changes.why: Stable since 7.4 and the assumed idiom in current docs: every module references libs.spring.boot.starter.webmvc and the version exists in exactly one TOML file — with bundles for groups and plugin coordinates included. Renovate and Dependabot both understand the format.

code.now:
# gradle/libs.versions.toml
[versions]
kotlin = "2.4.10"
spring-boot = "4.1.0"

[libraries]
jooq = { module = "org.jooq:jooq" }  # version via Boot BOM

[plugins]
kotlin-jvm = { id = "org.jetbrains.kotlin.jvm", version.ref = "kotlin" }
spring-boot = { id = "org.springframework.boot", version.ref = "spring-boot" }

changes.title: Sharing build logic across modules
changes.now: Convention plugins in an included build-logic build
changes.was: allprojects { } / subprojects { } blocks reaching into other projects
changes.why: Cross-project configuration couples every module to the root script and is exactly what the configuration cache and isolated projects cannot track — the docs now call it discouraged. Gradle 9 made the cost concrete: builds that stay on allprojects forfeit the caching the 9.x line is built around. A convention plugin is the same code, owned as a plugin each module opts into.

changes.title: Reusing the configuration phase
changes.now: Configuration cache on — the preferred mode across 9.x
changes.was: Every invocation re-configured the entire build before running a task
changes.why: Stable in 8.1, preferred in 9.0, slated to become the default in Gradle 10: Gradle serialises the task graph and skips configuration entirely when nothing relevant changed — the difference between seconds and nothing on warm invocations. The blockers are plugins doing config-cache-unsupported things; the problems report names them.

code.now:
# gradle.properties
org.gradle.configuration-cache=true
org.gradle.configuration-cache.parallel=true
code.was:
$ gradle test
> Configure project :   (…every single time…)

changes.title: How reads hit the disk
changes.now: An asynchronous I/O subsystem — io_uring on Linux, visible in pg_aios
changes.was: Synchronous reads, issued one at a time per backend
changes.why: The headline of 18: sequential scans, bitmap heap scans and vacuum can keep many reads in flight, which is where the published multi-x read speedups come from. Mostly free at upgrade time — io_method and effective_io_concurrency are the tuning knobs if defaults disappoint.

changes.title: Planner statistics across a major upgrade
changes.now: pg_upgrade carries optimizer statistics over
changes.was: Every major upgrade began with an ANALYZE storm and a slow morning
changes.why: Until 18, pg_upgrade dropped planner statistics, so the hours after an upgrade ran on guesses. Statistics now survive the jump — removing the main operational excuse for postponing majors.

changes.title: Generating primary-key UUIDs
changes.now: uuidv7() — time-ordered, so B-tree-friendly
changes.was: gen_random_uuid() (v4) — random, so index-hostile at scale
changes.why: Random v4 keys scatter inserts across the whole index; v7 keys are time-prefixed, so new rows land in the same hot pages and range scans over recent data stay cheap — the ULID idea, standardised (RFC 9562) and in core.

changes.title: Insert-or-update-or-delete in one statement
changes.now: MERGE — multiple WHEN clauses, one pass
changes.was: Writable-CTE contortions once the logic outgrew ON CONFLICT
changes.why: For the plain two-case upsert, INSERT … ON CONFLICT remains the right (and concurrency-safer) tool. MERGE earns its keep when the decision table grows — matched-and-stale → update, matched-and-gone → delete, not-matched → insert — which previously meant chained CTEs or application loops.

code.now:
MERGE INTO inventory i
USING incoming s ON i.sku = s.sku
WHEN MATCHED AND s.qty = 0 THEN DELETE
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET qty = s.qty
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (sku, qty) VALUES (s.sku, s.qty);
code.was:
WITH upd AS (
  UPDATE inventory i SET qty = s.qty
  FROM incoming s WHERE i.sku = s.sku
  RETURNING i.sku
)
INSERT INTO inventory (sku, qty)
SELECT sku, qty FROM incoming
WHERE sku NOT IN (SELECT sku FROM upd);
-- and the delete case still isn't handled

changes.title: Turning a JSON document into rows
changes.now: JSON_TABLE() — declare columns, get a relation
changes.was: jsonb_array_elements() chains with lateral joins and casts
changes.why: The SQL/JSON standard's answer to shredding documents: one call declares the paths, types and nested structure, and the result is an ordinary relation you can join. The old idiom worked but buried the schema in a pile of operators.

code.was:
SELECT o.id,
       l->>'sku' AS sku,
       (l->>'qty')::int AS qty
FROM orders o,
LATERAL jsonb_array_elements(o.payload->'lines') AS l;

changes.title: Computed columns
changes.now: Virtual generated columns — computed on read, stored nowhere
changes.was: STORED generated columns, or triggers keeping a real column in sync
changes.why: Since 12, generated columns had to be STORED — paid for on every write and in every row's bytes. 18 adds the virtual kind: the expression evaluates at read time, which is usually what a derived display value wanted all along.

code.now:
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN total_display numeric
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (subtotal + tax) VIRTUAL;
code.was:
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN total_display numeric
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (subtotal + tax) STORED;

changes.title: Multicolumn indexes without the leading column
changes.now: B-tree skip scan: (tenant_id, created_at) serves WHERE created_at > …
changes.was: A second single-column index, or a sequential scan
changes.why: The old rule — a composite index is useless unless the query constrains its leading column — softened in 18: when the leading column is low-cardinality, the planner can iterate its values and dive the index per value. Fewer redundant indexes, less write amplification.

changes.title: Seeing before and after in one write
changes.now: RETURNING old.balance, new.balance on UPDATE/INSERT/DELETE/MERGE
changes.was: A prior SELECT, or a trigger writing an audit row, to capture the previous value
changes.why: Audit trails and optimistic-concurrency checks kept re-reading rows around writes. 18 lets the write itself report both versions atomically.

code.was:
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 7;  -- hope nothing changes
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 50 WHERE id = 7;

changes.title: Backups between the full ones
changes.now: pg_basebackup --incremental, reassembled with pg_combinebackup
changes.was: Full base backups plus WAL archives — storage and restore time paid in full
changes.why: 17's WAL summarizer lets a base backup contain only pages changed since a previous one, cutting both backup storage and the nightly window; pg_combinebackup reconstructs a full backup from the chain at restore time.

changes.title: How migrations run in Boot 4
changes.now: spring-boot-starter-flyway (or -liquibase) — explicit
changes.was: flyway-core on the classpath was enough to run on startup
changes.why: Boot 4's modularization moved Flyway/Liquibase autoconfiguration into their own starters. Same behaviour once present — migrations on startup against the app DataSource — but presence is now an explicit dependency choice instead of a classpath side effect.

changes.title: Generating the schema classes
changes.now: The official jooq-codegen-gradle plugin, run against a migrated database
changes.was: Community Gradle plugins with drifting configuration models
changes.why: Codegen is jOOQ's foundation — the generated tables are what make queries type-checked — and since 3.19 the Gradle plugin is first-party, so its configuration tracks the tool instead of chasing it. Point it at a database your migrations just built and commit the output.

changes.title: jOOQ from suspend functions
changes.now: jooq-kotlin-coroutines — transactionCoroutine over the R2DBC integration
changes.was: runBlocking bridges wrapped around the blocking API
changes.why: The coroutine module suspends over jOOQ's reactive (R2DBC) execution rather than parking threads. With virtual threads the plain blocking API inside a coroutine dispatcher is also legitimate — pick one bridge per codebase, not both.

changes.title: Fetching a parent with its children
changes.now: MULTISET subqueries mapped to nested data classes — one query, one round trip
changes.was: JOIN + groupBy in memory, N+1 loops, or an ORM entity graph
changes.why: MULTISET turns a correlated subquery into a typed nested collection, serialised by the database (SQL/JSON underneath) and deserialised straight into your DTO shape. The flat-join-then-regroup dance — and its duplicated parent rows — disappears, without adopting an ORM's change tracking.

code.now:
val orders: List<OrderWithLines> = dsl
    .select(
        ORDERS.ID,
        ORDERS.PLACED_AT,
        multiset(
            select(ORDER_LINES.SKU, ORDER_LINES.QTY)
            .from(ORDER_LINES)
            .where(ORDER_LINES.ORDER_ID.eq(ORDERS.ID))
        ).convertFrom { it.map(mapping(::Line)) }
    )
    .from(ORDERS)
    .where(ORDERS.CUSTOMER_ID.eq(customerId))
    .fetch(mapping(::OrderWithLines))
code.was:
val rows = dsl.select(ORDERS.ID, ORDERS.PLACED_AT,
        ORDER_LINES.SKU, ORDER_LINES.QTY)
    .from(ORDERS)
    .leftJoin(ORDER_LINES).on(ORDER_LINES.ORDER_ID.eq(ORDERS.ID))
    .where(ORDERS.CUSTOMER_ID.eq(customerId))
    .fetch()

val orders = rows.groupBy { it[ORDERS.ID] }   // parent repeated per line
    .map { (_, group) -> group.toOrderWithLines() }

changes.title: Walking foreign keys in a query
changes.now: Path joins: ORDERS.customer().NAME — to-one and, since 3.19, to-many
changes.was: An explicit JOIN … ON for every hop
changes.why: The generated code knows the foreign keys, so the query can walk them as properties; jOOQ synthesises the joins. To-one paths came earlier; 3.19 extended paths to to-many (and many-to-many) relationships, which pairs naturally with MULTISET for the child collections.

code.now:
dsl.select(ORDERS.ID, ORDERS.customer().NAME)
   .from(ORDERS)
   .where(ORDERS.customer().TIER.eq("GOLD"))
   .fetch()
code.was:
dsl.select(ORDERS.ID, CUSTOMERS.NAME)
   .from(ORDERS)
   .join(CUSTOMERS).on(CUSTOMERS.ID.eq(ORDERS.CUSTOMER_ID))
   .where(CUSTOMERS.TIER.eq("GOLD"))
   .fetch()
